takeaways: A linear two-port with no internal sources fixes two relations among V₁, I₁, V₂ and I₂, so any two of them can be chosen as the free pair; each choice is a parameter set of four constants.
Draw both port currents entering the network. Then a load gives V₂ = −I₂Z<sub>L</sub> and the power into the two-port is V₁I₁ + V₂I₂.
Z parameters need an open circuit at the far port, Y parameters a short circuit, h parameters one of each; ABCD uses the output open (A, C) and shorted (B, D).
Every set follows from another by algebra; a conversion exists only when the parameter it divides by is not zero.
Series connections add Z matrices and parallel connections add Y matrices only if the port condition survives the wiring; cascades multiply ABCD matrices in signal order with no extra condition.
Reciprocity (z₁₂ = z₂₁, AD − BC = 1) holds for any network of R, L, C and coupled coils; symmetry (z₁₁ = z₂₂, A = D) is a separate property.

A driving-point function is realizable with passive elements only if it is positive real; LC and RC functions have simple, alternating poles and zeros, and Foster and Cauer forms turn them into circuits with the same number of elements.

bank.q: Define a port and a two-port network. State the port condition and the sign convention for the four port variables, explain why a linear two-port needs only four parameters, and list the parameter sets with their free variables.
outline: Port: a terminal pair with equal and opposite currents
Two-port: ports 1–1′ and 2–2′; three-terminal networks qualify
Convention: V across each port, both currents entering; load gives V₂ = −I₂Z<sub>L</sub>
Linear, no independent sources, zero initial energy
Four variables, two relations, two free variables, four constants
Six sets: Z, Y, h, g, ABCD, inverse ABCD
answer: Port. A port is a pair of terminals through which the current entering one terminal equals the current leaving the other (the port condition). A port therefore carries one voltage and one current.

Two-port. A two-port network has two such pairs: port 1 (terminals 1–1′, the input) and port 2 (terminals 2–2′, the output). A three-terminal network with 1′ and 2′ joined, such as a T network or a transistor, is still a two-port: its common terminal returns both port currents.

Sign convention. V₁ is the voltage of terminal 1 with respect to 1′ and V₂ that of 2 with respect to 2′. I₁ enters terminal 1 and I₂ enters terminal 2: both currents are drawn into the network. The power entering the two-port is P = V₁I₁ + V₂I₂, and a load ZL at port 2 obeys V₂ = −I₂ZL.
Conditions for fixed parameters. The network must be linear, contain no independent sources, and start with no stored energy. Dependent sources are allowed.

Why four parameters. There are four port variables, but the network imposes two linear relations among them. So two variables are free and two are dependent; each dependent variable is a linear combination of the two free ones, with two constants each: four constants in all.

y₁₁ = z₂₂/Δz     y₁₂ = −z₁₂/Δz
y₂₁ = −z₂₁/Δz    y₂₂ = z₁₁/Δz

answer: T network, Z tests. Port 2 open: I₁ flows through 2 Ω and 4 Ω, so V₁ = 6I₁ and V₂ = 4I₁ (no drop on the idle 3 Ω arm): z₁₁ = 6 Ω, z₂₁ = 4 Ω. Port 1 open: I₂ flows through 3 Ω and 4 Ω, so V₂ = 7I₂ and V₁ = 4I₂: z₂₂ = 7 Ω, z₁₂ = 4 Ω.
Determinant. Δz = 6 × 7 − 4 × 4 = 42 − 16 = 26 Ω². (For any T network Δz = Z₁Z₂ + Z₂Z₃ + Z₃Z₁ = 6 + 12 + 8 = 26 Ω² ✓.)

answer.text: Y parameters.

answer: Direct check of y₁₁ and y₂₁. Short port 2 and apply V₁ = 1 V. Port 1 sees 2 + (3 ∥ 4) = 2 + 1.7143 = 3.7143 Ω, so I₁ = 0.2692 A ✓. The centre node is at 1 − 2 × 0.2692 = 0.4615 V and the current through the 3 Ω arm into the short is 0.1538 A, leaving terminal 2; so I₂ = −0.1538 A and y₂₁ = −0.1538 S ✓.
Direct check of y₂₂. Short port 1 and apply 1 V at port 2: port 2 sees 3 + (2 ∥ 4) = 4.3333 Ω, so y₂₂ = 1/4.3333 = 0.2308 S ✓.

Remarks. y₁₂ = y₂₁ because z₁₂ = z₂₁ (the network is reciprocal). The negative sign of y₂₁ is physical: the short draws current out of terminal 2. Note that y₁₁ ≠ 1/z₁₁ (1/6 = 0.1667 S): the input impedance with the output shorted (3.7143 Ω) differs from that with the output open (6 Ω).

Closing check. [Z][Y] should be the unit matrix: first row times first column = 6 × 0.2692 + 4 × (−0.1538) = 1.615 − 0.615 = 1.000, and first row times second column = 6 × (−0.1538) + 4 × 0.2308 = −0.923 + 0.923 = 0 ✓.

answer: Reciprocity. A network is reciprocal when exchanging the positions of an ideal source and an ideal meter leaves the reading unchanged. For a two-port: a current I into port 1 gives an open-circuit voltage z₂₁I at port 2, and the same current into port 2 gives z₁₂I at port 1. Reciprocity means these are equal: z₁₂ = z₂₁. Every linear network of R, L, C, coupled coils and ideal transformers is reciprocal; dependent sources usually break it.
Y form. y₁₂ = −z₁₂/Δz and y₂₁ = −z₂₁/Δz, so z₁₂ = z₂₁ gives y₁₂ = y₂₁.
h form. h₁₂ = z₁₂/z₂₂ and h₂₁ = −z₂₁/z₂₂, so z₁₂ = z₂₁ gives h₁₂ = −h₂₁. The minus sign comes from the short-circuit test for h₂₁, in which the current flows out of terminal 2.

Symmetry. A two-port is symmetric when its ports can be exchanged without any change at the terminals; then the open-circuit impedances are equal, z₁₁ = z₂₂.

Z<sub>in</sub> = (AZ<sub>L</sub> + B)/(CZ<sub>L</sub> + D) = 4.673 Ω
Gain 0.167 = product of the stage gains
Reduction check

answer.text: Cascade. [T] = [T][T]:

answer: Reciprocity check. AD − BC = 3.875 × 4.6875 − 21.125 × 0.8125 = 18.164 − 17.164 = 1 ✓: a cascade of reciprocal networks is reciprocal. It is not symmetric (A ≠ D).

bank.q: Test whether Z(s) = (s² + 1)(s² + 4)/[s(s² + 2)] is an LC driving-point impedance, and realize it in Foster I, Foster II, Cauer I and Cauer II forms. Draw the Foster II and Cauer II networks.
outline: Poles 0, ±j√2, ∞; zeros ±j1, ±j2; alternate
Foster I: partial fractions of Z
Foster II: partial fractions of Y
Cauer I: continued fraction in descending powers
Cauer II: continued fraction in ascending powers
Check: four elements in each; Z(j1) = 0
answer: Pole-zero test. Numerator (s² + 1)(s² + 4) = s⁴ + 5s² + 4 is even; denominator s(s² + 2) = s³ + 2s is odd; degrees differ by one. Zeros at ω = 1 and 2 rad/s; poles at 0, √2 = 1.414 rad/s and ∞. On the jω axis: pole 0, zero 1, pole 1.414, zero 2, pole ∞. They alternate and are simple, so Z(s) is an LC impedance (positive residues are confirmed below).

answer.text: Foster I. Partial fractions of Z(s):
answer.pre:
k∞ = 1 (ratio of leading coefficients)
k₀ = [sZ(s)] at s = 0 = 4/2 = 2
2k₁ = [(s² + 2)Z(s)/s] at s² = −2 = (−1)(2)/(−2) = 1
Z(s) = s + 2/s + s/(s² + 2)

answer: Elements in series: L = 1 H; C = 1/2 F (from 2/s); a parallel tank with C = 1/(2k₁) = 1 F and L = 2k₁/ω₁² = 1/2 H.

answer.text: Foster II. Partial fractions of Y(s) = s(s² + 2)/[(s² + 1)(s² + 4)]:

answer: Each term 2ks/(s² + ω²) is a series LC branch with L = 1/(2k) and C = 2k/ω²: branch 1, L = 3 H and C = 1/3 F; branch 2, L = 3/2 H and C = (2/3)/4 = 1/6 F. The two branches are in parallel.

answer.text: Cauer I (remove the pole at ∞; descending powers):
answer.pre:
(s⁴ + 5s² + 4) ÷ (s³ + 2s) = s,   remainder 3s² + 4   → series L₁ = 1 H
(s³ + 2s) ÷ (3s² + 4) = s/3,     remainder 2s/3     → shunt C₂ = 1/3 F
(3s² + 4) ÷ (2s/3) = 9s/2,       remainder 4        → series L₃ = 9/2 H
(2s/3) ÷ 4 = s/6                                    → shunt C₄ = 1/6 F

answer.text: Cauer II (remove the pole at 0; ascending powers):
answer.pre:
(4 + 5s² + s⁴) ÷ (2s + s³) = 2/s,      remainder 3s² + s⁴  → series C₁ = 1/2 F
(2s + s³) ÷ (3s² + s⁴) = 2/(3s),       remainder s³/3     → shunt L₂ = 3/2 H
(3s² + s⁴) ÷ (s³/3) = 9/s,             remainder s⁴       → series C₃ = 1/9 F
(s³/3) ÷ s⁴ = 1/(3s)                                      → shunt L₄ = 3 H

bank.q: Explain the conditions under which the series, parallel and cascade interconnection rules are valid. Use two T networks (2 Ω, 3 Ω series arms, 4 Ω shunt arm) to show a series connection where the rule fails and one where it holds, describe the Brune test, and show why the parallel and cascade rules hold for such networks.
outline: Series: currents common, voltages add, Z add, port condition
Parallel: voltages common, currents add, Y add
Cascade: product, no condition
Grounded T networks in series: second network shorted, true Z = [11.2 9.2; 9.2 12.2] Ω
Turned over: Z = [12 8; 8 14] Ω
Brune test: junction voltage zero
Isolating transformer
answer: Series. In a series connection the same current flows through port 1 of both networks and through port 2 of both, and the port voltages add. Then [V] = [Zₐ][I] + [Zᵦ][I], so [Z] = [Zₐ] + [Zᵦ]. This needs each network to keep its port condition after the wiring: the current entering terminal 1 of a network must leave by its own terminal 1′.

Parallel. In a parallel connection both networks see the same V₁ and V₂ and the currents add, so [Y] = [Yₐ] + [Yᵦ]. This needs no circulating current between the networks through their return terminals.
Cascade. [T] = [Tₐ][Tᵦ] needs no extra condition, because the current leaving port 2 of one network is, by the wiring, the current entering port 1 of the next.

answer.text: Series, done wrongly. Take two grounded T networks (common terminal at the bottom) and join 1′ of a to 1 of b and 2′ of a to 2 of b. Network a's common wire now also joins terminals 1 and 2 of b, so the 2 Ω and 3 Ω arms of b are in parallel and b collapses to one impedance in the common lead:

answer: The rule would have given [Zₐ] + [Zᵦ] = [12 8; 8 14] Ω, which is wrong: the port currents of b are not I₁ and I₂ any more.

answer.text: Series, done rightly. Turn network b over, so its common terminal is at the top and meets the common terminal of a. Now only the two common terminals are joined, each network still carries I₁ through its port 1 and I₂ through its port 2, and

answer: Check of z₁₁: with port 2 open, I₁ runs through 2 + 4 Ω of a and 4 + 2 Ω of b: 12 Ω ✓. Check of z₁₂: a current into port 2 passes through both 4 Ω shunt arms, and port 1 reads that drop: 8 Ω ✓.

svg.aria: Left: two T networks with their common terminals both at the bottom; the common wire of a shorts terminals 1 and 2 of b, so the series rule fails. Right: network b turned over so the two common terminals meet; the rule holds.

answer: Brune test. Connect port 1 of the two networks in series as intended, drive it with I₁, and leave the port-2 junction open (do not join 2′ of a to 2 of b). The voltage across that gap must be zero; if it is not, joining the gap makes a current circulate. In the wrong arrangement, with I₁ = 1 A, terminal 2′ of a is at the potential of terminal 1 of b, and terminal 2 of b sits z₁₁ − z₂₁ = 6 − 4 = 2 V away from it: the gap has 2 V, so the test fails. In the right arrangement both sides of the gap are the joined common terminals: 0 V, so the test passes. The same test with the ports exchanged is also needed.

Parallel and cascade for these networks. Two grounded three-terminal networks in parallel share their common terminal anyway, so no current can circulate and the Y rule always holds (for example the bridged-T: T network plus a 5 Ω bridge gives [0.4692 −0.3538; −0.3538 0.4308] S). Cascade never needs a check: two T networks in cascade give [1.5 6.5; 0.25 1.75]² = [3.875 21.125; 0.8125 4.6875].
Fix when the test fails. An ideal 1 : 1 isolating transformer at one port of one network forces equal and opposite currents in that port's terminals, so the rule then holds.
Closing check. The wrong-arrangement matrix is still reciprocal (9.2 = 9.2) and its z₁₁ = 11.2 Ω equals 6 Ω (network a) plus the 5.2 Ω common-lead impedance, as the collapsed circuit predicts.

bank.q: State the conditions for a driving-point function to be positive real and the properties of LC and RC impedances. Judge each of the following and realize those that are LC or RC: (a) (s + 2)/(s + 1); (b) (s + 1)/(s + 2); (c) (s² + 4)/[s(s² + 1)]; (d) (s² + 1)/(s² + 4); (e) (s² + 3s + 2)/(s² + s + 1).
outline: PR: real for real s, no RHP poles or zeros, simple jω poles with positive residues, Re Z(jω) ≥ 0
LC: simple alternating poles and zeros on the jω axis
RC: alternating on the negative real axis, pole nearest the origin
(a) RC, (b) RL not RC, (c) not PR, (d) not PR, (e) PR but needs R, L and C
answer: Positive-real conditions. Z(s) is real for real s; it has no poles or zeros with Re s > 0 (numerator and denominator Hurwitz); any pole on the jω axis, including s = 0 and s = ∞, is simple with a real positive residue; and Re Z(jω) ≥ 0 for every ω. Only PR functions can be built from passive elements.

LC impedance. An odd rational function (even over odd or odd over even, degrees differing by one); simple poles and zeros on the jω axis that alternate; a critical frequency at s = 0 and at s = ∞; Re Z(jω) = 0.
RC impedance. Simple poles and zeros on the negative real axis that alternate; the critical frequency nearest the origin is a pole and the farthest is a zero, so Z(0) > Z(∞); all residues positive.

answer.text: (a) Z = (s + 2)/(s + 1). Pole −1, zero −2: alternating, pole nearest the origin; Z(0) = 2 Ω > Z(∞) = 1 Ω. An RC impedance:
answer.pre: Z = 1 + 1/(s + 1)  → 1 Ω in series with (R = 1 Ω ∥ C = 1 F)

answer.text: (b) Z = (s + 1)/(s + 2). Zero −1 is nearest the origin and Z(0) = 0.5 Ω < Z(∞) = 1 Ω, so it is not an RC impedance (its RC expansion 1 − 1/(s + 2) has a negative residue). It is PR, and it is an RL impedance:

answer: Check: a parallel RL has Z = Rs/(s + R/L); with R = 0.5 Ω and R/L = 2, L = 0.25 H ✓. At s = 0 the inductor shorts the 0.5 Ω, leaving 0.5 Ω = Z(0) ✓.

answer.text: (c) Z = (s² + 4)/[s(s² + 1)]. Poles 0, ±j1; zeros ±j2. On the jω axis: pole 0, pole 1, zero 2: two poles in a row, so not LC. The residue at s² = −1 is negative:

answer: A jω-axis pole with a negative residue fails the PR test: not realizable. (Its reciprocal is an LC impedance, so it is an LC admittance.)

answer.text: (d) Z = (s² + 1)/(s² + 4). Even function, so not LC. On the jω axis Z(jω) = (1 − ω²)/(4 − ω²) is real:

answer: Re Z(jω) < 0 for 1 < ω < 2 rad/s, so Z is not PR and no passive network has it.

answer.text: (e) Z = (s² + 3s + 2)/(s² + s + 1). Numerator roots −1, −2; denominator roots −0.5 ± j0.866 (left half plane): both Hurwitz. On the jω axis:

answer: Z is PR (for example Re Z(j1) = 3 and Re Z(j2) = 18/13 = 1.385). Its poles are complex, so it is neither LC nor RC: a realization needs R, L and C together (Brune's method or an RLC ladder).

answer.text: Verdict.

answer: Closing check. For (a), Z(1) = 3/2 = 1.5 Ω and the network gives 1 + 1/(1 + 1) = 1.5 Ω ✓. For (b), Z(1) = 2/3 Ω and the network gives 0.5 + 0.5 × 1/(1 + 2) = 0.667 Ω ✓.

glossary.def: A pair of terminals through which the current entering one terminal equals the current leaving the other.
A network with an input port and an output port, described by two linear equations in V₁, I₁, V₂ and I₂.
The requirement that each port carries equal and opposite currents in its two terminals.
The Z parameters, each measured with the other port open.
The Y parameters, each measured with the other port shorted.
The h parameters, with I₁ and V₂ as free variables; used for transistors.
The g parameters, with V₁ and I₂ as free variables; [g] = [h]⁻¹.
The ABCD (chain) parameters: V₁ = AV₂ − BI₂, I₁ = CV₂ − DI₂.
The set giving V₂ and I₂ in terms of V₁ and −I₁; the inverse of the ABCD matrix.
The ratio V/I at one port, with the other port in a stated condition.
The ratio of a voltage at one port to a current at the other, such as z₂₁.
A two-port with a source impedance at port 1 and a load at port 2.
A network whose transfer is the same in both directions: z₁₂ = z₂₁, AD − BC = 1.
A network whose ports can be exchanged without any change at the terminals: z₁₁ = z₂₂, A = D.
Two two-ports with common port currents and added port voltages; their Z matrices add.
Two two-ports with common port voltages and added port currents; their Y matrices add.
Port 2 of one two-port feeding port 1 of the next; their ABCD matrices multiply.
A check that a series or parallel connection keeps every port condition, made by measuring the voltage across the open junction.
A function real for real s with Re Z(s) ≥ 0 for Re s ≥ 0; the condition for passive realizability.
A polynomial with no roots in the right half of the s plane.
The driving-point impedance of an LC network; an odd rational function with alternating poles and zeros on the jω axis.
A realization from the partial fractions of Z(s) (first form, series elements) or Y(s) (second form, parallel branches).
A ladder realization from a continued fraction, removing poles at infinity (first form) or at zero (second form).
A chain of alternating series and shunt arms.
